processing: Yunnan large-leaf is withered, broken into small particles, often on crush-tear-curl (CTC) lines, then oxidised, dried and graded by particle size.
harvest_season: Dian Hong picking runs from about mid-March to mid-November, across spring, summer and autumn teas.
appearance_dry: Even, tight, heavy granules, dark with a brown cast.
appearance_wet: Fine particles of an even, bright red.
taste_profile: Strong, fresh and brisk with a clean aroma, built to carry milk and sugar.

brewing.notes: Western style or a tea bag, in boiling water. It brews fast, and past about 3 minutes it turns harsh. Takes milk well.

vintage_note: An everyday blending tea, not sold by vintage. Grades matter more than years: one major maker sorts its CTC into numbers 1 to 6 by particle size. Buy recent stock and use it within a year or two, since the small particles go flat quickly.
description:
Broken Dian Hong is the working side of Yunnan black tea. Dian Hong comes in two main forms, gongfu with whole strips and broken graded tea; this is the second, meant for strength rather than for a slow session.

Large-leaf Yunnan tea is cut small, today often by CTC machine, oxidised and sorted by size. More broken surface means quicker extraction, so you get a strong, red cup in a couple of minutes.

The flavour is bold and brisk, with a clean aroma and enough backbone for milk. Boiling water and one short steep are all it wants; keep steeping it and it becomes rough.

You'll meet it mostly in tea bags, milk tea and blends. Look at the grade, since particle size changes both speed and strength, and fine dust is the lowest end.

For a clear lesson in what processing does, brew it alongside a gongfu Dian Hong from the same region.
history: The Fengqing factory, forerunner of today's Dianhong Group, is the best-documented maker. It began producing CTC broken tea in 1992 on a complete line imported from India, and in 2003 added three more lines, reaching an annual capacity of 2,500 tons.
